posts.name: Rahul
posts.cooked: Normal regex in bash for such requirement with egrep is '(\b\w+\b)\s+\1' or '(\b\w+\b) \1'. But is this valid for gawk? The backreferences will work in gawk?

posts.name: Swati Jain
posts.cooked: Yes, backreferences like \1 work in gawk, but only inside functions like match() and not directly in pattern regex literals. For portability, use POSIX classes ([[:space:]], [[:alnum:]]) instead of \s and \w.

posts.name: Rahul
posts.cooked:
Whether this exception was taught anywhere during course, handbook, revision classes, practice session.

Moreover after using the charater classes also same as given in end term I am not able to get the desires output

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
If your lines are just two words, then simply do

awk '$1 == $2'

If it contains variable words,

awk '{
  for (i = 1; i < NF; i++) {
    if ($i == $(i+1)) {
      print
      break
    }
  }
}' pairs

Dont really need regex here.

However, yes if you are asking about backreferences, they do not work in awk, either in the ruleset, or even in match() as well. awk uses a regex parsing engine that is faster than perl because it does not include support for backreference (which makes it slower).

Awk does not support backreferences in a regexp because to do so would require a much slower regexp engine than awk uses (see https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html) and it’s not necessary and rarely desired.

However, you can use match to store the results in an array and compare that.

gawk '{
  if (match($0, /([[:alnum:]_]+)[[:space:]]+([[:alnum:]_]+)/, m)) {
    if (m[1] == m[2]) print
  }
}' pairs
